content: Tobacco smoking during pregnancy is one of the few preventable factors associated with complications in pregnancy and has significant long-term consequences for both mothers and their babies. While smoking during pregnancy is decreasing in high-income countries, it remains strongly linked to poverty and is increasing in lowand middle-income countries. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of smoking cessation interventions during pregnancy on smoking behavior and perinatal health outcomes. The review included randomized controlled trials, cluster-randomized trials, and quasi-randomized controlled trials that focused on psychosocial interventions to help pregnant women stop smoking. A total of 102 trials with 120 intervention arms were included, involving over 28,000 women. The interventions were categorized into counseling, health education, feedback, incentives, social support, exercise, and dissemination. High-quality evidence demonstrated that counseling significantly increased smoking cessation rates in late pregnancy compared to usual care (30 studies; average risk ratio [RR] 1.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.19 to 1.73) and less intensive interventions (18 studies; average RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.47). However, it was uncertain whether counseling was effective when provided as part of a broader maternal health intervention or when comparing different types of counseling. Counseling also showed a clear effect on smoking abstinence at 0 to 5 months postpartum (11 studies; average RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.26 to 2.01) and at 12 to 17 months postpartum (2 studies; average RR 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.96), with a borderline effect at 6 to 11 months postpartum (6 studies; average RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.77). Health education showed a borderline effect compared to usual care (5 studies; average RR 1.59, 95% CI 0.99 to 2.55), but the evidence was downgraded to moderate quality. The effect was unclear when health education was compared to less intensive interventions (4 studies; average RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.70) or when it was part of a broader maternal health intervention. Feedback interventions, when combined with other strategies such as counseling, significantly increased smoking cessation rates compared to usual care (average RR 4.39, 95% CI 1.89 to 10.21). However, the evidence was downgraded to moderate quality due to the small number of studies (2 studies). The effect of feedback was uncertain when compared to less intensive interventions (3 studies; average RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.75 to 2.20). Incentive-based interventions were found to be highly effective when compared to alternative (non-contingent incentive) interventions (4 studies; RR 2.36, 95% CI 1.36 to 4.09). However, pooled effects could not be calculated for comparisons with usual care or less intensive interventions due to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 93%). The effect of social support interventions was unclear. Support provided by peers (6 studies; average RR 1.42, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.07), by partners (1 study), or as part of a broader maternal health intervention did not show consistent results. Similarly, the effect of exercise interventions (1 study; RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.72 to 2.01) and dissemination of counseling (1 study; RR 1.63, 95% CI 0.62 to 4.32) was unclear. Importantly, high-quality evidence showed that psychosocial interventions led to a 17% reduction in the number of infants born with low birthweight, a significantly higher mean birthweight (mean difference [MD] 55.60 g, 95% CI 29.82 to 81.38 g), and a 22% reduction in neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions. However, the effects on preterm births and stillbirths were unclear. There were no adverse psychological effects associated with the interventions. Over time, the intensity of support provided in both intervention and comparison groups has increased. Higher-intensity interventions were more likely to have higher-intensity comparisons, which may explain why no clear differences were observed with increasing intervention intensity in meta-regression analyses. Studies with unclear implementation and unequal baseline characteristics were less effective. There was no clear difference in effectiveness between trials conducted by researchers (efficacy studies) and those implemented by routine pregnancy staff (effectiveness studies). However, there was uncertainty in the effectiveness of counseling in four dissemination trials where the intervention focus was at an organizational level. The pooled effects were similar for women of predominantly low socioeconomic status compared to other women. The interventions were effective among women from ethnic minority groups but not among indigenous women. Similar effect sizes were observed in trials with biochemically validated smoking abstinence and those with self-reported abstinence. It was unclear whether incorporating self-help manuals or telephone support increased the effectiveness of interventions. In conclusion, psychosocial interventions, particularly counseling, feedback, and incentives, can help pregnant women stop smoking and improve perinatal outcomes, such as reducing low birthweight and NICU admissions. However, the effectiveness of health education and social support remains less clear. The characteristics and context of the interventions should be carefully considered when designing and implementing smoking cessation programs for pregnant women.
